sections.title: Purpose and Scope of Manual
sections.summary: Micropiles have been used since the 1950s, mainly as foundation support against static and seismic loads and less often as in-situ reinforcement of slopes and excavations. The 1993 FHWA state-of-the-practice review (FHWA, 1997) led to the 2000 Implementation Manual; this manual revises the 2001 Implementation Manual, with changes listed by chapter (sonic drilling, corrosion protection per DFI 2003, a design flowchart, FS for grout-ground bond reduced from 2.5 to 2.0, buckling, seismic design, slope design steps, PDA and Statnamic testing, costs).
sections.body: (pp. 1-1 to 1-3) The use of micropiles has grown significantly since their conception in the 1950s, and particularly since the mid-1980s. They have been used mainly as foundation support elements resisting static and seismic loads and, to a lesser extent, as in-situ reinforcement stabilizing slopes and excavations, many for transportation structures. In 1993 FHWA sponsored a review of the state of the practice by contractors, consultants, academics and owners; the resulting Drilled and Grouted Micropiles - State-of-the-Practice Review (FHWA, 1997) reviewed research, testing, design methods, construction, site observations and monitored case studies, evaluated limitations and uncertainties, and identified the need for a design and construction manual for highway agency geotechnical and structural engineers. FHWA then sponsored Micropile Design and Construction Guidelines, Implementation Manual (FHWA, 2000), a cooperative effort of FHWA, U.S. micropile specialty contractors and several state DOTs, intended as a practitioner-oriented document on design, construction specifications, inspection and testing, cost data and contracting methods. This manual revises the 2001 Implementation Manual. Major revisions: Chapter 3, updated and added case histories on evaluating micropile feasibility; Chapter 4, sonic drilling; Chapter 5, corrosion protection updated to current FHWA practice and the levels of protection of the DFI Guide to Drafting a Specification for High Capacity Drilled and Grouted Micropiles for Structural Support (DFI, 2003), a design flowchart covering the structural and geotechnical strength and service limit states, guidance on subsurface investigation (depth and spacing of borings), the factor of safety for grout-ground bond reduced from 2.5 to 2.0 to reflect current practice (with the rationale), geotechnical strength limit states (compression, uplift, downdrag), combined axial compression and bending, buckling, lateral loading and the capacity at a threaded connection, battered micropiles, group settlement and group lateral movement, and seismic design using FOREVER (2003) research and the Japanese Public Works Research Institute (2002) manual; Chapter 6, feasibility for slope stabilization with the geotechnical parameters needed and the method's limitations, three case histories, and a step-by-step method covering micropile location, passive resistance in front of the micropiles, axial load transfer, and the iterative analysis above and below the slip surface; Chapter 7, evaluations for a verification and proof testing program, PDA and Statnamic testing for quality assurance; Chapter 8, an inspector responsibilities checklist and an updated installation log; Chapter 10, updated cost estimating (steel, labor, load testing) and typical measurement and payment items.
key_points: Micropiles used since the 1950s, mainly as foundation support for static and seismic loads, less often as in-situ slope and excavation reinforcement
FHWA 1993 state-of-the-practice review published as FHWA (1997); Implementation Manual FHWA (2000)
This manual revises the 2001 Implementation Manual
Ch 5 revisions: DFI (2003) corrosion protection levels, design flowchart, boring depth and spacing guidance
Factor of safety for grout-ground bond reduced from 2.5 to 2.0 to reflect current practice
Ch 5 adds downdrag, combined compression and bending, buckling, lateral loading, threaded joints, group settlement and seismic design (FOREVER 2003; Japanese PWRI 2002)
Ch 6: slope stabilization feasibility, three case histories, step-by-step iterative design above and below the slip surface
Ch 7: verification and proof test programs, PDA and Statnamic testing; Ch 8: inspector checklist and installation log; Ch 10: costs, measurement and payment

sections.title: Micropile Definition and Description
sections.summary: A micropile is a small-diameter (typically less than 300 mm (12 in.)) drilled and grouted non-displacement pile, typically reinforced: drill, place steel, grout (Figure 1-1). It carries significant axial and moderate lateral loads, with minimal disturbance, in restricted access and all ground types, at any angle below horizontal. High-capacity steel resists most or all of the load; special drilling and grouting give high grout/ground bond; end bearing is generally neglected.
sections.body: (pp. 1-4 to 1-5) A micropile is a small-diameter (typically less than 300 mm (12 in.)), drilled and grouted non-displacement pile that is typically reinforced. It is constructed by drilling a borehole, placing steel reinforcement and grouting the hole (Figure 1-1). Micropiles can withstand relatively significant axial loads and moderate lateral loads, and may substitute for conventional driven piles or drilled shafts or act as one component of a composite soil/pile mass, depending on the design concept. They are installed by methods causing minimal disturbance to adjacent structures, soil and the environment, where access is restrictive, in all soil types and ground conditions, and at any angle below the horizontal with the equipment used for ground anchors and grouting. Because installation causes minimal vibration and noise and works in low headroom, micropiles are often used to underpin existing structures, often with specialized drilling equipment inside basements or other limited-headroom facilities. On conventional cast-in-place drilled or non-displacement piles most of the load is resisted by the reinforced concrete, and capacity rises with cross-sectional and surface area; micropile structural capacity instead relies on high-capacity steel elements resisting most or all of the load, occupying as much as one-half of the drillhole cross section. The special drilling and grouting methods allow high grout/ground bond values; the grout transfers load through friction from the reinforcement to the ground in the bond zone, much as in ground anchors. Because of the small diameter, any end-bearing contribution is generally neglected. The grout/ground bond strength depends primarily on the ground type and the grouting method (pressure grouting or gravity feed); the drilling method also matters, though it is less well quantified.
key_points: Micropile: small-diameter (typically < 300 mm (12 in.)), drilled and grouted non-displacement pile, typically reinforced
Construction: drill a borehole, place steel reinforcement, grout (Figure 1-1)
Resists relatively significant axial loads and moderate lateral loads; substitute for driven piles or drilled shafts, or part of a soil/pile composite
Installed with minimal disturbance, in restricted access and low headroom, in all ground types, at any angle below horizontal
Structural capacity relies on high-capacity steel, which may occupy up to one-half of the drillhole cross section
Load transferred by grout/ground bond friction in the bond zone, as in ground anchors; end bearing generally neglected
Bond strength depends primarily on ground type and grouting method (pressure or gravity); drilling method also influential

sections.title: Historical Background
sections.summary: Micropiles were conceived in Italy in the early 1950s for underpinning historic buildings damaged over time and in World War II: Fondedile (technical director Dr. Fernando Lizzi) developed the palo radice (root pile) (Figure 1-2). Load tests exceeded 400 kN (90 kips) against design estimates under 100 kN (23 kips), with no grout/ground bond failures. Reticulated networks followed from 1957 (Figure 1-3). UK 1962, Germany 1965, North America 1973; U.S. growth from the mid-1980s.
sections.body: (pp. 1-5 to 1-8) Micropiles were conceived in Italy in the early 1950s in response to the demand for innovative underpinning of historic buildings and monuments damaged with time, especially during World War II; the system had to support structural loads with minimal movement and be installed in access-restrictive environments with minimal disturbance. The Italian specialty contractor Fondedile, whose technical director was Dr. Fernando Lizzi, developed the palo radice, or root pile: a small-diameter, drilled, cast-in-place, lightly reinforced, grouted pile (classic underpinning arrangement, Figure 1-2). Steel was scarce in postwar Europe but labor was inexpensive, abundant and skilled, encouraging these lightly reinforced elements, largely designed and installed by specialty contractors on a design-build basis. Load tests measured capacities in excess of 400 kN (90 kips), although contemporary bored pile methods suggested less than 100 kN (23 kips); full-scale load tests were cheap, so much test information was acquired and published, and no grout/ground bond failures were recorded in these early tests. Root piles spread in Italy through the 1950s; Fondedile introduced them in the United Kingdom in 1962 for underpinning historic structures, and by 1965 they were used in Germany on underground urban transportation projects, when for proprietary reasons 'micropile' replaced 'root pile'. Most early applications were structural underpinning in urban environments. Starting in 1957, reticoli di pali radice (reticulated root piles) were introduced: multiple vertical and inclined micropiles interlocked in a three-dimensional network forming a laterally confined soil/pile composite (Figure 1-3), used for slope stabilization, quay wall reinforcement, protection of buried structures and other soil and structure support. Other proprietary micropiles were developed in Switzerland and Germany and exported by branches or licensees; portions of Asia became a major market. Fondedile introduced micropiles in North America in 1973 with underpinning in the New York and Boston areas, but U.S. use grew rapidly only from the mid-1980s, when published case histories, specialty contractors and the needs of consultants and owners in old urban environments overcame the skepticism of the traditional East Coast piling market (Bruce, 1988).
key_points: Conceived in Italy in the early 1950s for underpinning historic buildings and monuments (damage over time and in World War II)
Fondedile (technical director Dr. Fernando Lizzi) developed the palo radice (root pile): small-diameter, drilled, cast-in-place, lightly reinforced, grouted
Early load tests exceeded 400 kN (90 kips) against bored pile estimates under 100 kN (23 kips); no grout/ground bond failures recorded
Introduced in the UK in 1962 and Germany by 1965, when 'micropile' replaced 'root pile'
Reticulated root piles (reticoli di pali radice) from 1957: 3-D networks of vertical and inclined micropiles forming a confined soil/pile composite
Introduced in North America in 1973 (New York and Boston); U.S. growth from the mid-1980s (Bruce, 1988)
